sections: I think the market is significantly undervaluing Samsung Electronics. Given the likely long-term supply-demand tightness in memory, Samsung's position as the DRAM market leader, the potential for a breakthrough in HBM market share, 60%-70% of capacity locked in through long-term contracts (a mid-to-long-term plan), aggressive progress in the foundry business (expected to turn profitable by 2027), and an extremely large amount of free cash flow, the market should assign Samsung Electronics a higher valuation multiple to correct this mispricing.

1. The detailed reasons for why memory could face long-term supply-demand tightness have already been covered in my analyses of MU and SNDK, so I won't elaborate much here (AI's insatiable appetite for KV cache + the HBM wafer penalty + HBM yield ramps getting progressively harder + effectively no meaningful new capacity coming online before 2028).

2. First, let me state upfront: I'm essentially treating Samsung Electronics as a pure memory play with a small foundry component bolted on, stripping out all the other miscellaneous businesses (which don't make much money anyway). Everything below is analyzed on this basis.

Samsung is the DRAM market leader. In this cycle it actually commands even stronger pricing power than SK Hynix and Micron (though because of market dynamics, Samsung, Micron, and Hynix are now essentially aligned — something like the oligopoly competition you see in economics).

Samsung's DS division posted total operating profit of ₩89 trillion, an operating margin of 70%. Given that the other two businesses within DS carry lower margins, the memory segment's operating margin must be well above 70%. Let me back out the memory-specific margins roughly: Samsung's memory division generated revenue of roughly ₩120.8 trillion in 2026Q2, and memory almost certainly accounted for nearly all of DS's operating profit. Under my own assumption, Samsung's memory operating margin is around 74% — and given that the foundry division isn't yet profitable, I may actually be underestimating Samsung's memory operating margin. Samsung's net profit in 2026Q2 was ₩71.27 trillion, almost 100% of which came from memory, implying a memory net margin of around 60% (these figures serve as an anchor point for the valuation later).

Yet the industry leader hasn't earned a premium relative to its competitors, for two reasons: 1) memory gross margins are already close to a ceiling, especially given that downstream phone and PC shipments are starting to feel the pinch from memory price hikes (the clearest evidence being that Samsung's own phone and PC businesses have started to post losses); 2) Samsung is not the leader in HBM — its market share there trails Hynix by a wide margin. Samsung currently holds about 38% of the overall DRAM market, but only just over 20% in HBM, far below SK Hynix's roughly 60% share.

Over the next few quarters, a slowdown in DRAM and NAND growth rates is essentially a given, since price hikes on the consumer-electronics side are close to their ceiling. Whether Samsung can further push up its gross and net margins will depend heavily on whether it can achieve a breakthrough in HBM market share. (I've made this argument before in my Micron note: the fact that per-bit margins are currently higher for conventional DRAM than for HBM doesn't make economic sense. Over the coming quarters HBM should get repriced — in theory, per-bit HBM economics should eventually surpass DRAM.)

According to the latest credible reports, Samsung's HBM4 yield has already exceeded 80%, ramping up far faster than during the HBM3E era. Samsung was also the first company to deliver HBM4E samples, and it's using its own 4nm process for the base die (theoretically superior in performance).

Taken together, these signals suggest Samsung has a real shot at finally breaking out of its long-standing stagnant HBM market share. I don't think it can overtake Hynix — the recent trip by Samsung and Hynix to the US to meet with and sign agreements with tech giants shows Hynix still holds a commanding lead in HBM, and that lead isn't just about performance; it's also about customer trust. But climbing above its prior ~21% share would still be significant progress.

Assume Samsung's HBM share reaches 30% by 2027 (with Hynix at 50% and Micron at 20% in the same period). Based on forecasts from multiple investment banks and the broader market, the HBM market is expected to exceed $100 billion in 2027 and could reach $150–200 billion by 2028. That 9-point share gain would translate into roughly $7 billion in extra operating profit for Samsung in 2027 and over $10 billion in 2028, which would further support Samsung's valuation.

My own caveat: I actually don't hold out much hope for a major breakthrough in Samsung's HBM market share — my own estimate above reflects that. I also think any improvement in Samsung's valuation will come mostly from a higher multiple rather than from earnings growth. The profit contribution from a higher HBM share is actually quite limited. But a higher share does help drive multiple expansion, because HBM has been the biggest beneficiary of this AI wave and is also the product best positioned to resist cyclical repricing.

3. Samsung's long-term agreements (LTAs) are a critical piece of the re-rating story. I've already covered LTAs in detail in my MU and SNDK notes — memory makers' current LTAs generally set a floor and a ceiling price, with the floor-price gross margin exceeding the peak of any prior cycle.

Samsung has already signed LTAs with 5 major global data-center customers, and is in final-stage negotiations with 5 more large AI-related customers (almost every major customer is now asking for multi-year supply agreements, and some existing customers are seeking additional volume). Samsung's mid-to-long-term target is to lock in 60%-70% of output through LTAs.

Samsung's LTAs have already received prepayments amounting to roughly a quarter of the total committed value, and future contracts should expand prepayments further. If Samsung can eventually push the prepayment ratio up to around 30%, the probability of counterparty default should fall sharply (I won't repeat the detail here — it's covered in my two SNDK notes). Based on a rough calculation, as long as spot prices don't fall by half, the probability of renegotiation is small — and in my view, the odds of spot prices falling by half by 2028 are not high.

Samsung's operating profit for H1 was ₩147 trillion; a conservative full-year estimate would be ₩350 trillion (~$250 billion). A conservative estimate for 2027 operating profit would be $360 billion (KB Securities forecasts Samsung's 2027 operating profit at ₩575 trillion — I've already discounted that. And $360 billion in operating profit only implies 44% growth over 2026, i.e., a 15% increase in shipments and a 30% increase in price — a completely reasonable, if anything slightly conservative, estimate).

For SNDK I used a 9-10x forward P/E. Applying the same approach to Samsung would put its market cap at roughly $2.8 trillion. For Micron I used 15x 2028 net profit under an assumption of a 50% crash in memory prices; applying the same method, my estimate for Samsung's 2028 operating profit comes to above $234 billion (I assume Samsung's LTAs will likely cover a larger share of shipments, so I'm estimating 2028 revenue at 65% of 2027's — also factoring in higher depreciation — which is on the conservative side). That implies net profit of roughly $187 billion, which again lands at a $2.8 trillion valuation.

Applying a Korea discount, I'll knock 20% off that, bringing it to a still-remarkable $2.24 trillion. Rounding down further (giving Samsung a bit of an unfair haircut), Samsung's market cap should still be around $2 trillion, implying a share price of ₩472,000. The current share price is a severe departure from the real fundamentals — and this is without even factoring in the progress Samsung has made in foundry.

4. Samsung has made a real breakthrough in foundry. It has already signed foundry deals with Tesla for both AI5 and AI6 (AI5 tape-out is complete; AI6 has been signed, worth $16.5 billion total, running through 2033), plus new orders from Nvidia (autonomous driving) and Groq (AI chips), among others.

Many analysts expect Samsung's foundry share to stabilize around 8-9% by mid-2027, but getting above 10% would require 2-3 successful 2nm customer tape-outs, which likely wouldn't materialize until 2027-2028.

Either way, this is a free call option. TSMC's supply is currently nowhere near sufficient to meet market demand, and if Samsung can capture some of that overflow demand, it means meaningful incremental revenue and profit — plus the customer trust earned from seizing this opportunity could feed back into Samsung's continued expansion in memory. (As mentioned earlier, Samsung's DS division generates close to ₩10 trillion in revenue outside of memory, and I estimate foundry accounts for the majority of that — at least 60%. If the foundry business can achieve a 30% operating margin, factoring in Samsung's growing market share, this segment could start contributing an extra $5 billion in operating profit out of nowhere starting in 2028 — a meaningful incremental gain.)

5. Samsung's shareholder return policy for FY2024-FY2026 is ₩9.8 trillion in dividends plus 50% of free cash flow (with a portion potentially returned via means other than dividends). If Samsung can offer even greater shareholder returns going forward — say, large-scale buybacks like SanDisk — its EPS could rise further on top of this (given the sheer scale of Samsung's cash flow, buybacks would deliver a meaningful EPS boost), which would in turn help push the share price higher.

• ☐Whether Samsung can raise its HBM market share (breaking above the market consensus figure of ~21%)
  • ☐Whether Samsung can hit its own target of covering 60%-70% of memory shipments through LTAs
  • ☐Whether Samsung's foundry business continues to win orders from major customers
  • ☐Whether Samsung can stay ahead of — or maintain a lead in — HBM4E
  • ☐Whether Samsung strictly executes its shareholder return plan and further expands it going forward (i.e., whether it sticks to returning 50% of FCF to shareholders while also expanding returns through other means)

If any of the following happen, I'll admit I was wrong:

  1. Samsung not only fails to lead in HBM4E but continues to fall further behind Hynix
  2. Samsung's HBM market share fails to increase
  3. Samsung fails to achieve the LTA coverage ratio that management has guided to
  4. Samsung fails to win new large-customer orders in foundry
  5. Samsung fails to strictly execute its policy of returning 50% of FCF to shareholders, and doesn't introduce additional forms of shareholder returns going forward

What the market thinks: Samsung Electronics is a traditional cyclical stock.

Why I disagree: DRAM plus enterprise SSDs are becoming less cyclical (helped by LTAs), turning into an indispensable strategic resource for AI infrastructure — and Samsung is the leader in memory. On top of that, Samsung holds a free call option in the form of foundry, with substantial upside potential, and its valuation is likely to be re-rated.
